passages.happening:
‘Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He stirred up David against them’ (verse 1), to take a census of Israel and Judah.

David tells Joab, the commander of his army, to go through all the tribes from Dan to Beersheba and count the fighting men, ‘so that I may know their number’ (verse 2). Joab objects: “May the LORD your God multiply the troops a hundred times over, and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?” (verse 3). ‘Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army’ (verse 4).

So Joab and the commanders go. They cross the Jordan to Aroer and Gad, go north through Gilead to Dan and around toward Sidon and the fortress of Tyre, then south to the Negev and Beersheba. After nine months and twenty days they come back to Jerusalem. ‘In Israel there were 800,000 men of valor who drew the sword, and in Judah there were 500,000’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Second Samuel ends not with a triumph but with a sin, a judgment and an altar. This chapter pairs with chapter 21: both begin with a disaster on the land traced to the LORD's response to a king's sin, and both end with God answering prayer for the land. The census probably took place late in David's reign, when his kingdom had reached its widest extent.

The route traces a great loop: east across the Jordan, north through Gilead to Dan and toward the Phoenician coast, then down to the Negev and Beersheba in the far south. Dan to Beersheba was the old way of naming the whole land.

Why was the census wrong? The text does not say directly, and interpreters have given several reasons. Counting fighting men was the first step toward conscription and taxation, and it could show a king trusting in his army rather than in God. Israel belonged to the LORD, not to the king, and counting it as the king's resource may have been presumption. And the law required a ransom for each person counted in a census, so that no plague would come; some connect that law with the plague here. Joab, not a man known for scruples, saw the danger at once.

Chronicles gives different totals, 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah. Some think different things were counted; others see separate sources, or the copying slips common in large numbers. The site's page on the numbers in Samuel and Chronicles sets them out.
passages.later:
The law of the census said, ‘each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered’ (Exodus 30:12).

Chronicles tells the same story and names another as the one who moved David: “Then Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to take a census of Israel” (1 Chronicles 21:1).
passages.hard:
If the LORD stirred David up to take the census, why was David punished?

The chapter says that the LORD's anger burned against Israel and that he stirred David up, and that raises hard questions of justice. First Chronicles retells the event and names Satan as the one who incited David, and many interpreters read the two accounts together. On that reading God permitted, or used, an adversary's temptation as part of a judgment already due for some sin of Israel the text does not name, while David freely chose his act and answered for it.

Others note that ancient Hebrew often speaks of everything, even what God permits, as God's own doing, in keeping with his rule over all things. The verb for stirring up is used for enticing someone toward harm. Here the LORD is its subject, and in Chronicles the same verb has Satan as its subject. The two accounts together show the Bible speaking of God's rule and a hostile power's work in the same event, without making God the author of sin. The chapter does not settle every question.
passages.asks: David wanted to know the size of his strength. Ask where you are tempted to measure your security by numbers, money or influence rather than by trust in God. And ask who around you, like Joab, is asking the question you would rather not hear.

passages.happening:
Once the count is done, David's conscience strikes him. He says to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly” (verse 10).

In the morning the word of the LORD comes to Gad the prophet, David's seer. He brings David three choices: three years of famine, three months of fleeing from his enemies, or three days of plague (verse 13). David answered Gad, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men” (verse 14).

So the LORD sends a plague on Israel, ‘and seventy thousand of the people from Dan to Beersheba died’ (verse 15). But when the angel stretches out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relents and says to the angel, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” (verse 16). The angel is standing by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David sees the angel striking down the people, he says to the LORD, “Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This time David confesses before any prophet confronts him.

Gad was David's seer, a prophet who had been with him since his years in the wilderness. The three choices shrink in length and grow in force: three years, three months, three days. David chooses to fall into the hands of the LORD rather than of men, because God's mercies are great.

The angel is stopped at Jerusalem. The word for relented means to be sorry, or to change course. God changes course in response to what he sees, not because he was wrong, but because mercy belongs to his character.

Verse 17 is the turn of the chapter. For the first time in it David sees the people as sheep and himself as the shepherd who is guilty, and he asks that the punishment fall on him and his family. In this chapter repentance is not only sorrow. It is the willingness to bear the cost.
passages.later: Chronicles has David say the same: ‘Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great’ (1 Chronicles 21:13). And the prophets would later say of the LORD, ‘He relents from sending disaster’ (Joel 2:13).
passages.hard:
Why did the people die for the king's sin?

The text ties their suffering both to the LORD's anger against Israel at the start of the chapter and to David's sin, and it also shows God cutting the plague short in mercy. David himself protests the injustice to the sheep, and the Bible lets his protest stand. The chapter does not resolve every question. It holds God's rule, human responsibility and God's mercy together.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David asked that the punishment fall on him and not on the people. Ask what responsible leadership looks like when your choices have hurt others. And ask whether you are willing to bear the cost yourself rather than let it fall on those in your care.

passages.happening:
That day Gad tells David to go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David goes. Araunah sees the king coming and bows to the ground, and asks why he has come. “To buy your threshing floor,” David replied, “that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted” (verse 21).

Araunah offers it all as a gift: the floor, the oxen for a burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and yokes for wood (verse 22). “No,” replied the king, “I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing” (verse 24). David buys the floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. He builds an altar there and offers burnt offerings and peace offerings. ‘Then the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and the plague upon Israel was halted’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
A threshing floor was a flat, hard, open place, often on high ground to catch the wind, where harvested grain was beaten out and winnowed. It was a natural place for gatherings and sometimes for worship. The sledges and yokes were wooden farm tools that could be burned as fuel for the sacrifice.

Araunah was a Jebusite, one of the people who held Jerusalem before David took it, so Jebusites still lived and owned land in the city. He offers everything for nothing. David will not worship God with what costs him nothing. True worship involves real sacrifice, not the use of someone else's gift.

Burnt offerings were wholly burned on the altar, and they spoke of dedication and atonement. Peace offerings were shared meals that celebrated fellowship restored with God. The plague ends through an altar and sacrifices offered at the place God chose.

Chronicles gives a different price, six hundred shekels of gold for the whole site. Some think Samuel prices the floor and the oxen and Chronicles the whole area; others see separate sources or copying variation.

So the book that began with Saul's death ends by preparing the ground, quite literally, for the house of God. The next book will build it here.
passages.later: Chronicles names what was built on this ground: ‘Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David. This was the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite’ (2 Chronicles 3:1). It also says that God answered David's offering with fire: ‘He called upon the LORD, who answered him with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering’ (1 Chronicles 21:26).
passages.asks: David would not offer God what cost him nothing. Ask what costly worship or generosity would look like in your life right now. And ask whether there is something you have been giving God only because it was free.
